fields.meaning:
～も・・・だし、～もまた・・・だ
Both... and...
examples: At the venue, there were both single people and married people.
That restaurant has good food and a nice atmosphere, and on top of that, the prices are reasonable.
He is good at sports, and he also plays the piano like a pro.
I disliked studying and was bad at sports, so naturally my grades were poor too.
At home, we have neither an air conditioner nor a microwave.
*That parent doesn't even try to correct their child when the child is bothering others. Honestly, like parent, like child.

fields.meaning: Not… at all, not the least bit…
examples: Don't worry. I'm not sick or anything.
This shop isn't cheap or anything, yet it's always crowded.
That's not love or anything of the sort. It's just obsession.
He's no hero or anything. He's an ordinary person.
It's a result that isn't particularly special at all.
fields.explain:
Spoken language, direct; it can feel like a strong, rather blunt denial. Use with care in formal writing.
“でも” means “or something similar,” widening the coverage of the negation; “も” emphasizes “not even …”.
Often used to reassure, clear up a misunderstanding, or rebut an opinion.

• Emphatic negative phrase: “not … or anything,” “not … at all.”
• The form “Nでもなんでもない” is very common; “Nもなんでもない” also occurs but is less common, with a blunt, outspoken nuance.
• With adjectives, the structure emphasizes the degree “not at all”: 高くもなんでもない（not expensive at all）, 怖くもなんでもない（not scary in the least）.
fields.notes:
• The double emphatic form “XでもYでもなんでもない” negates all options: 若さでも実力でもなんでもない.
• With i-adjectives, there is a variant that sounds more natural in some regions: ～くもなんともない (～なんともない means “it's nothing / no problem at all”).
• In conversation, a strong fall in intonation at the end strengthens the nuance of rebuttal.
mistakes: Using “Nもなんでもない” in formal settings sounds blunt; switch to “Nではない／Nとは言えない”.
Confusing it with standalone “なんでもない” meaning “it's nothing / it's fine”: 痛くもなんでもない（doesn't hurt at all） is different from なんでもない（it's fine）。
The JLPT often tests recognizing the broad scope of negation created by “でも”: compared with 全然～ない, it is a negation that lists multiple options.

examples: Life has both failures and successes.
This job has its fun times and its tough times.
Japan has both tradition and innovation.
Some shops are cheap, and some are expensive.
Like parent, like child.
fields.explain:
Often used with ある/いる/起こる/見られる to state that two sides exist.
To emphasize strong criticism, use the frame “NもNならNもNだ”.
N can be replaced by a noun phrase: ～こともあれば～こともある.

• Lists two parallel sides: there is both A and B; sometimes with the nuance “there is this, and there is also that.”
• The “NもNならNもNだ” type usually carries an evaluation (often negative): “as A is, so is B.”
• Often used to state general characteristics or give a balanced comment (pros/cons) about a target.
fields.notes:
• The “Vば” form in this pattern appears mostly as “ある/いる/起こる…”; with other verbs, it usually switches to a nominalization: ～こともあれば～こともある.
• The phrase “NもNならNもNだ” can occasionally be used positively, but it usually expresses criticism.
• Flexible translations: “also… also…”, “sometimes… sometimes…”, “both… and…”. meaning_vi: not only ～ but also ～ ⏐ explain: Adds a matter in the same direction as the preceding one. (good – good, bad – bad) ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は勉強もできればスポーツもできる。
He is good at studying and good at sports too.
2. 私は歌も下手ならダンスも下手だ。
I'm bad at singing and bad at dancing too.
mistakes: Using an い形容詞 with ければ in this frame: × 安ければ高いも → say 安い店もあれば高い店もある instead.
Confusing it with ～たり～たり: when saying “sometimes… sometimes…”, both are correct, but ～も～ば～も～ leans toward existence/general characteristics.
Forgetting to repeat “も”: × 山もあれば海ある → ○ 山もあれば海もある.

fields.meaning: Even if one wants to…, still…
fields.connection: V volitional form + にも + [cannot] (行こうにも時間がない)
examples: Even if I wanted to contact them, I don't know the phone number.
Even if I wanted to go to the venue, public transportation has stopped.
Even if I wanted to apologize, I have no chance to see him.
Even if I want to forget it, I can't forget it that easily.
Even if I wanted to apply, the deadline has already passed.
fields.explain:
Used when tools/information are lacking: 連絡先がない／手段がない／時間がない.
Moderately formal; can be used in both written and spoken language.
The second clause is usually: 〜ない／難しい／無理だ／困難だ.

～ようにも expresses the situation “even if you want/intend to do V, you cannot, or it is very difficult” because of a lack of conditions or means, or an objective obstacle. “にも” emphasizes a hypothetical effort that is impossible.
• Usually accompanied by a second clause that is negative or describes an obstacle.
• Creates a feeling of “helplessness” in the face of circumstances rather than subjective unwillingness.
fields.notes:
• The second clause can be omitted if the context is clear: 金がなくて、行こうにも…。 (spoken language)
• Often used with verbs of perception/emotion: 忘れる／笑う／泣く.
• In formal writing, the second clause uses an abstract noun: 〜に障害がある／〜に支障を来す.
mistakes: Using “ようにも” with an affirmative second clause → logically wrong (行こうにも時間がある → contradictory).
Confusing it with “ようと”: “ようにも” means “even if you want to…”, while “ようと〜まいと” means “whether or not”.
Dropping “にも”: 連絡しように… → incorrect; it must be 連絡しようにも…

fields.meaning: Cannot… even if one wants to…
fields.connection: V volitional form + にも + V potential form ない (読もうにも読めない)
examples: There are memories I can't forget even if I try to.
The venue is packed, so I can't get in even if I want to.
I'm sleepy, yet even if I try to sleep, I can't.
I can't contact him even if I want to. That's because I lost his number.
The atmosphere was such that you couldn't laugh even if you wanted to.
fields.explain:
Used for difficulties that are objective rather than subjective.
More formal than “VたくてもVない”.
Suitable for written language, journalism, and theses when you need to emphasize impossibility.

Expresses “even if you want/intend to do V, you cannot do V.” The reason is an objective limitation (lack of conditions, prohibition, health, distance, etc.). Emphasizes helplessness in the face of circumstances.
• Form that repeats the same verb: Vようにも V-可能形-ない.
• The second clause is always the negative potential form of that same verb.
fields.notes:
• Avoid “ら抜き言葉” in standard language: 見れない → use 見られない instead.
• Often used with verbs of perception/emotion: 忘れる／笑う／泣く／動く.
• The second clause can also use the passive-potential structure: 〜られない.
mistakes: Not repeating the same verb: 忘れようにも考えられない → incorrect; it must be 忘れようにも忘れられない.
Using the affirmative in the second clause → incorrect: 会おうにも会える.
Using the wrong potential form of する/来る: しようにもしれない → incorrect; it must be しようにもできない. 来ようにも来れない (colloquial) → use 来られない in standard language.

fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + ようもない (連絡しようもない)
examples: I don't know his address or phone number, so there's no way to contact him.
There are no clues, so there's no way to investigate the case.
This stain is too old; there's no way to get it out.
The explanation is vague, so there's no way to understand it.
It's encrypted, so there's no way to recover the data.
fields.explain:
Used when something is objectively impossible, not because the speaker doesn't want to.
Decisive, strong nuance; suitable for written language and reports.
With emotions: 「言いようもない」= not knowing how to put it properly (a literary aura).

～ようもない expresses “there is no way / it is impossible to do V” because of a lack of information, tools, or conditions. The degree of impossibility is stronger than “〜にくい/づらい”.
• The focus is on “there is no method.”
• Often used with nouns giving the reason: 連絡先／手がかり／手段／方法／証拠.
fields.notes:
• “どうしようもない” is a common set phrase: to be at a loss / to have no options left.
• Often used in investigation reports, QA, and IT: 再現しようもない／検証しようもない.
• Do not confuse it with “〜しかない” (the only option left) — the meanings are opposite.
mistakes: Wrong verb form: using V辞書形 + ようもない → incorrect; it must be V-ます with ます dropped.
Using it when other options still remain → a semantic contradiction.
Confusing it with “〜にくい”: “ようもない” means impossible due to a lack of method, not just “difficult”.

rows: Almost synonymous with ようもない

examples: He quit the company without consulting anyone.
She left the room without saying a single word.
They kept working without resting.
You must not view the data without obtaining permission.
He finished the project without making any mistakes.
Going into a presentation without any preparation is reckless.
fields.explain:
Suitable for formal documents, reports, and academic writing.
Emphasizes that action A “absolutely did not happen”; stronger than ～ないで／～ずに.
Often used when A is something one would normally do, but the speaker emphasizes that it was not done.

• Expresses doing action B while not doing action A (V-る) at all.
• Highly formal; often used in reports, articles, and narratives.
• Often used with frequency-emphasizing words “一度も／少しも／まったく”.
• V-る must be a normally expected action that here “did not happen.”
fields.notes:
• In policy/regulation texts, ことなしに creates a serious tone: 許可を得ることなしに～は禁止する。
• Combined with evaluative expressions: ～ことなしに済む（get by without having to do A）.
• When you want to sound gentle, consider ～ないで／～ずに; when you need formality/emphasis, use ～ことなしに／～ことなく.
mistakes: Using it for an action that is not clearly “habitual/expected” → the sentence sounds less natural (the pattern emphasizes “A should have been done”).
Confusing it with ～ないで: exams often test the formal nuance; choose ～ことなしに/ことなく for written language.
Using the wrong form: V-ない + ことなしに（×）; the correct form is V-る + ことなしに.
Overusing it in everyday conversation -> sounds stiff; switch to ～ないで／～ずに.

fields.meaning: So as not to…, to avoid…
examples: Please double-check before submitting so that you don't make any mistakes.
We will strictly enforce safety standards so that no accidents occur.
Please be careful with your wording so as not to cause misunderstandings.
I had my child carry a tag with our contact information so that they wouldn't get lost.
We will review the system so that we never make the same mistake again.
Put on a scarf before you go out so you don't catch a cold.
fields.explain:
Formal; often used in instructions, internal notices, and signs.
Focuses on the preventive goal; the second clause states a clear measure/suggestion.
Can be used as a modifier: ～ことのないよう注意書き（a notice so that … does not happen）

• “So as not to …”, “in order to avoid …”: expresses a goal/prevention so that something bad does not happen.
• Ceremonious, formal nuance; suited to notices/instructions/policies.
• Often accompanied by a request, suggestion, or concrete measure in the second clause.
fields.notes:
• The phrase “二度と～ことのないように” is very common in letters of apology and corrective-action reports.
• On signs: 火事の起きることのないように → 火事を起こさないように (shorter), depending on the level of formality.
• Can stand at the beginning of a sentence as a subordinate clause: ～ことのないように、関係各所に周知した。
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ことがない (almost never) → a completely different meaning.
Putting an adjective/noun directly before ことのないように → incorrect; it must be a verb in the V-る form.
Omitting the measure/suggestion in the second clause makes the sentence unnatural in instructions.

rows: General, less formal; common in everyday conversation.
<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れないようにメモする。

<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えぬように<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>をつける。
Emphasizes a clear purpose-reason relationship; more rational nuance.

fields.meaning: The more you…, the more endless it gets
examples: If you start listing his faults, there's no end to them.
If I start counting up the things I want, there's no end to it.
Once I start talking about this topic, there's no end to it, so let's stop here.
If I listed all the good points of the menu, there would be no end to it, but first, let me introduce the standard dishes.
If we start voicing our current complaints, there'll be no end to it, so let's focus on solutions.
Once you start looking for areas to improve, there's no end to it, but let's set priorities.
fields.explain:
A rhetorical nuance used to switch topics, wrap up an issue, and avoid rambling.
Often accompanied by から／ので to give the reason for stopping: ～ときりがないから／ので.
Suitable for both spoken and written language; in writing, it often appears with 挙げる・数える.

• If you start doing/mentioning V, it is “endless / there is no stopping point.”
• Used to cut things short or sum up: “there's a lot more to say, but let's stop here.”
• Often used when listing examples, complaints, wishes, pros/cons…
fields.notes:
• “きり” in きりがない = 切り（limit/boundary）; literal meaning: “there is no line marking the end.”
• Precede it with a listing phrase so the sentence sounds natural: 例を挙げるときりがない／数え上げればきりがない。
• Very handy for ending a rambling passage: ～ときりがないので、このあたりで切り上げます。
mistakes: Confusing “きり” with “切り/限り” in writing → note that きりがない is written in ひらがな in this pattern.
Using it with an unsuitable verb (one without a sense of listing/starting) makes the sentence unnatural.
Forgetting the conditional と／ば/たら → there must be a conditional clause before きりがない.

examples: Looking at this result, there's no need to explain the cause.
It's only drizzling, so there's no need to take a taxi. Let's walk.
It goes without saying that he is the best person for the job.
It's obvious at a glance. There's no need to run a test.
The meeting can be handled by email, so there's no need to go to the trouble of coming to the office.
fields.explain:
When emphasizing that something is “obvious”: often used with 当然・明らか・見れば分かる.
When emphasizing “not worth the effort”: used with わざわざ・わずか・この程度なら.
In formal written language, ～までもなく flows more smoothly mid-sentence.
After ～るまでもない, strong commands are not used; it suits mild recommendations/evaluations.

• Judges an action to be unnecessary: because it is too obvious, too simple, or not worth the cost/effort.
• Objective, polite nuance; used in both spoken and written language. 言うまでもない often comes at the beginning of a sentence that states something obvious.
• Different from なくてもいい: ～るまでもない usually implies “superfluous / no need because it is too obvious.”
fields.notes:
• “までも” originally means “to the extent that…”; combined with the negative “ない”, it creates the meaning “not to the point of having to…”.
• In reports, use “検討するまでもなく” when the conclusion is clear from the data.
• Avoid overusing it so as not to sound condescending in communication.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～なくてもいい: exams often ask you to choose the “obvious/superfluous” nuance → choose ～るまでもない.
Wrong form: it must be V-る + までもない; V-ない is not used.
“来なくてもいい” vs “来るまでもない”: the first gives permission not to come; the second implies “no need to come because it isn't worth it”.
Placing it after a noun is incorrect: ×予約までもない → 予約するまでもない.

rows: Neutral, gives permission; no implication of “obvious”.
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>はやらなくてもいい。
Polite/formal; means “no need to trouble anyone”.
